blocks.text: The locative answers *gdzie?*, “where?”, and *o kim? o czym?*, “about whom? about what?” It is the only Polish case that never appears without a preposition: it always follows *w*, *na*, *o*, *po* or *przy*.
The plural is easy (see below). The singular has two endings for masculine and neuter nouns and two for feminine nouns, and the choice depends on the last consonant of the stem.

head: ending
examples from the lessons
rows: masc. and neut., most hard stems
*Krakowie, telefonie, kinie, stole, mieście, powrocie, niebie, lecie*
masc. and neut. after k, g, ch
masc. and neut. after soft consonants and c, cz, sz, rz, ż
feminine, soft stems and c, cz, sz, rz, ż

blocks.text: The *-e* ending changes the consonant before it. These changes are regular, and once you know them the locative of almost any hard-stem noun is predictable:

head: change
examples
rows: feminine only: *rzeka → rzece, droga → drodze, mucha → musze*
*n, w, b, p, m, s, z* soften (written with *i*)

blocks.text: Watch the vowel too: *ó* often becomes *o* when the syllable opens (*Kraków → Krakowie*, *stół → stole*), and in a few words *a* becomes *e* (*miasto → mieście*, *lato → lecie*, *obiad → obiedzie*).
Every noun takes *-ach* in the locative plural, and every adjective *-ych* or *-ich*: *na światłach*, *w odwiedzinach*, *w nowych mieszkaniach*, *o polskich miastach*.

head: preposition
meaning
examples
rows: *w Krakowie, w pociągu, w telefonie, w środku*
*na stole, na dworcu, na konferencji, na światłach, na niebie*
*o panu, o czym, o którym rozmawialiśmy*

blocks.text: *O* and *po* also take the accusative, with a different meaning: *chodzi o wykład* (“it’s about”) and *iść po chleb* (“to fetch”). See the accusative page.
*W* is the default for enclosed spaces and for most towns and countries: *w Krakowie*, *w Polsce*, *w kinie*. *Na* is used for:

head: examples
rows: *na stole, na niebie, na ulicy, na Rynku*

blocks.text: The choice of *w* or *na* also fixes the matching words for “to” and “from”:
So *w* pairs with *do* + genitive, and *na* pairs with *na* + accusative. *Z* + genitive serves both.
Some time expressions use *w* + locative: *w tym tygodniu*, “this week”; *w zeszłym roku*, “last year”; *w lecie*, “in summer” (also *latem*); *w nocy*, “at night.”
